Everybody calls me Jamie.

Hello. Thanks for visiting my webpage. I'm a computer science researcher based in Scotland. I got a PhD from Cambridge University in 2001 on the foundations of computation, which introduced "Nominal techniques" <seo>(based on the Gabbay-Pitts model of names in Fraenkel-Mostowski sets)</seo>. This won some prizes.

Nowadays I work on the logic and topological structure of decentralised systems and cryptography; I am very pleased to have applied logic to both. I'm also interested in slide rules, game of life, and other things. I have a wheat intolerance and I do editorial work in academic publishing.

Research

My work connects mathematical logic and theoretical computer science, from the structure of names and binding to models of decentralised action. Click on a topic to jump to papers on that topic.

  • Decentralised systems

    Semitopology, blockchain models and mathematical structures for cooperation without central control.

    • Algebras of UTxO blockchains
    • Semitopology
    • Semiframes

  • Cryptography

    Arithmetisation of first-order logic and cryptographic proofs over finite models.

    • zkFOL paper
    • zkFOL code

  • И

    Nominal sets and foundations

    A mathematical account of names, binding, freshness, and alpha-equivalence, grounded in nominal sets and the Gabbay–Pitts model. The NEW quantifier И means “for a fresh name”.

    • Meet the NEW quantifier
    • PhD thesis
    • LICS 1999 paper
    • Journal paper

  • ⊢

    Logic and proof theory

    Nominal algebra, quantifiers, proof search, equational reasoning and the structure of logical derivations.

    • Nominal universal algebra
    • One-and-a-halfth-order logic
    • Quantifiers and proof-search

  • ⊨

    Semantics and duality

    Mathematical models of logic and computation, including nominal semantics, lattices, topology and representation theorems.

    • Semantics out of context
    • Lambda-calculus representation and duality
    • Stone duality with NEW

  • →

    Rewriting and unification

    Rewriting, substitution and unification in the presence of names, binding and alpha-equivalence.

    • Nominal unification
    • Nominal rewriting
    • Capture-avoiding substitution

  • λ

    Lambda calculus and metaprogramming

    Lambda-calculi, contexts, staged computation and syntax with meta-variables.

    • The lambda-context calculus
    • Contextual modal type theory
    • A nominal axiomatisation of the lambda-calculus

  • π

    Programming languages and processes

    Programming with binders, types, operational semantics and process calculi.

    • FreshML
    • Programming with bound names
    • The π-Calculus in FM

  3. Publication type: Journal article 2022

    Algebras of UTxO blockchains

    Murdoch J. Gabbay

    Mathematical Structures in Computer Science vol. 31, no. 9 In Homage to Martin Hofmann pp. 1034–1089 Cambridge University Press 2022-01 issue dated 2021-10 online 25 January 2022

    Murdoch J. Gabbay Mathematical Structures in Computer Science

    We condense the theory of UTxO blockchains down to a simple and compact set of four type equations (Idealised EUTxO), and to an algebraic characterisation (abstract chunk systems), and exhibit an adjoint pair of functors between them. This gives a novel account of the essential mathematical structures underlying blockchain technology, such as Bitcoin.

  1. Publication type: Conference paper 2020
    UTxO- vs account-based smart contract blockchain programming paradigms

    Lars Brünjes, Murdoch J. Gabbay

    Proceedings of the 9th International Symposium On Leveraging Applications of Formal Methods, Verification and Validation (ISOLA 2020) Springer 2020-10

    Lars Brünjes, Murdoch J. Gabbay Proceedings of the 9th International Symposium On Leveraging Applications of Formal Methods, Verification and Validation (ISOLA 2020)

    We implement two versions of a simple but illustrative smart contract: one in Solidity on the Ethereum blockchain platform, and one in Plutus on the Cardano platform, with annotated code excerpts and with source code attached. We prove some simple but novel results about observational equivalence and conclude with a wide-ranging and detailed discussion in the light of the examples, mathematical model, and mathematical results so far.

    A duality between partially ordered groups and an (apparently novel) category of partially ordered monoids and lazy homomorphisms between them. Every monoid can be lazily injected into a group.     Murdoch J. Gabbay Journal of Logic and Computation

    It is not obvious that Nominal Algebra is a pure equational logic, because of freshness conditions. E.g. η-conversion (eta-conversion) looks like this: a#X⊢λa.(Xa)=X. This is a conditional equality. The HSPA theorem for Nominal Algebra asserts that any model of a Nominal Algebra theory is part of a quotient of a product of atoms-abstractions of free models.

    Permissive Nominal Terms and their Unification

    Gilles Dowek, Murdoch J. Gabbay, Dominic P. Mulligan School of Mathematical and Computer Sciences, Heriot-Watt University

    We consider permissive nominal terms, and their unification. Permissive nominal terms closely resemble nominal terms, but they recover these useful ‘always fresh’ and ‘always alpha-rename’ properties, familiar from first-and higher- order syntax. In the permissive world, freshness contexts are elided, and the notion of unifier is based on substitution alone, rather than on nominal terms’ notion of substitution plus freshness conditions.

    We prove that expressivity is not lost moving to the permissive case and translate from nominal terms unification into permissive nominal terms unification.

    A logic of schematic reasoning based on nominal algebra. We give algebraic and sequent characterisations, and show correctness with respect to first-order logic. This subsumes the PPDP06 conference paper.

    Nominal algebra makes it easy to write axioms for capture-avoiding substitution—or does it? Consider the choices: do you want b[a↦X]=b or a#Z⊢Z[a↦X]=Z? Do you want Z[a↦a]=Z or not? In this paper we write down various plausible axioms and prove senses in which they are correct.

    Substitution for Fraenkel-Mostowski foundations

    Murdoch J. Gabbay, Michael J. Gabbay

    Proceedings of the 2008 AISB Symposium on Computing and Philosophy AISB 2008 Convention: Communication, Interaction and Social Intelligence vol. 12 pp. 65–72 University of Aberdeen, Aberdeen, UK: The Society for the Study of Artificial Intelligence and Simulation of Behaviour ISBN 1-902956-71-0 1 April 2008

    Murdoch J. Gabbay, Michael J. Gabbay Proceedings of the 2008 AISB Symposium on Computing and Philosophy

    We present a capture-avoiding substitution action defined in Fraenkel-Mostowski set theory on the entire sets universe. Substitution is commonly understood as an action on syntax (for example when building a logic or a lambda calculus) and thus as a prelude to, but not a part of, mathematical denotations. We show that it also has denotational realisation, as an operation on elements of a mathematical foundation.

    So nominal terms have two levels of variable. But that just means we have internalised the meta-level once. What if we do this repeatedly until we reach a fixedpoint?     Murdoch J. Gabbay School of Mathematical and Computer Sciences, Heriot-Watt University

    There are two natural ways of excluding an atom a in nominal techniques: we can consider the sets X such that a is fresh for X, or we can consider the sets X such that a is fresh for every x ∈ X. We show these lead to isomorphic categories. This can be read as saying that a fresh atom in the object-level is categorically isomorphic to a fresh atom in the meta-level.

    Permissive-nominal logic: First-order logic over nominal terms and sets

    Gilles Dowek, Murdoch J. Gabbay

    ACM Transactions on Computational Logic vol. 13, no. 3 pp. 1–36 article 20 New York: Association for Computing Machinery 1 August 2012

    Gilles Dowek, Murdoch J. Gabbay ACM Transactions on Computational Logic

    First-order logic with term-formers that can bind names. So we can axiomatise things like forall or lambda, or finitely axiomatise arithmetic. This gives PNL much of the expressive power of higher-order logic: but terms, derivations and models of PNL are first-order and the logic seems to strike a good balance between expressivity and simplicity. In brief, PNL is obtained by adding universal quantification to nominal algebra. But, to make that work we needed to invent permission sets.

    This is a journal version of the conference paper.

    Nominal Algebra and the HSP Theorem

    Murdoch J. Gabbay

    Journal of Logic and Computation vol. 19, no. 2 pp. 341–367 2009-04

    Murdoch J. Gabbay Journal of Logic and Computation

    It is not obvious that Nominal Algebra is a pure equational logic, because of freshness conditions. E.g. η-conversion (eta-conversion) looks like this: a#X⊢λa.(Xa)=X. This is a conditional equality. The HSPA theorem for Nominal Algebra asserts that any model of a Nominal Algebra theory is part of a quotient of a product of atoms-abstractions of free models.

    This limits the complexity of models, and puts a precise measure on the notion of equality of nominal algebra: making things equal, putting things into tuples, and forming atoms-abstracton.

    Permissive Nominal Terms and their Unification

    Gilles Dowek, Murdoch J. Gabbay, Dominic P. Mulligan

    School of Mathematical and Computer Sciences, Heriot-Watt University Technical Report no. HW-MACS-TR-0062 49 pp. total Edinburgh, UK 25 February 2009

    Gilles Dowek, Murdoch J. Gabbay, Dominic P. Mulligan School of Mathematical and Computer Sciences, Heriot-Watt University

    We consider permissive nominal terms, and their unification. Permissive nominal terms closely resemble nominal terms, but they recover these useful ‘always fresh’ and ‘always alpha-rename’ properties, familiar from first-and higher- order syntax. In the permissive world, freshness contexts are elided, and the notion of unifier is based on substitution alone, rather than on nominal terms’ notion of substitution plus freshness conditions.

    We prove that expressivity is not lost moving to the permissive case and translate from nominal terms unification into permissive nominal terms unification.

  1. Talk type: Conference talk 2025

    A declarative approach to specifying distributed algorithms using three-valued modal logic

    I discuss how to specify distributed protocols as axiomatic theories in three-valued modal logic. As usual for axiomatic (‘declarative’) specifications, this yields a compact, precise, easily-checkable summary of what the protocol is, while dispensing with algorithmic detail.

    Presented by Murdoch J. Gabbay 41st British Colloquium for Theoretical Computer Science (BCTCS 2025) Room TL325B, Learning and Teaching Building, University of Strathclyde Hosted by University of Strathclyde Glasgow, Scotland 16 April 2025

  2. Talk type: Conference talk 2025

    A shallow arithmetisation of first-order validity

    I discuss how to directly arithmetise (cryptographer-speak for ‘translate into polynomials, the language of cryptography’) validity over finite models. This means that you can specify a property – e.g. some desired correctness property – and via cryptographic magic generate succinct or zero-knowledge proofs that a model satisfies that correctness property, without communicating that model to the recipient of the proof. This is very useful, I would argue, for quickly proving correctness of data, behaviour, or anything else that can be finitely represented.

    Presented by Murdoch J. Gabbay 41st British Colloquium for Theoretical Computer Science (BCTCS 2025) Room TL325B, Learning and Teaching Building, University of Strathclyde Hosted by University of Strathclyde Glasgow, Scotland 15 April 2025

  3. Talk type: Workshop talk 2023

    Semitopologies and semiframes for distributed heterogeneous consensus

    A semitopology is like a topology, but without the restriction that an intersection of open sets needs to be open (this arises from modelling distributed systems). Semitopologies naturally generate a three-valued logic (by considering continuous functions out of them), and they can be dualised to semiframes, which are complete join-semilattices with a compatibility relation. We study these, along with various well-behavedness conditions on points in a semitopology.

    Presented by Murdoch J. Gabbay First Workshop on Heterogeneous Trust in Distributed Systems (HTDS 2023) Convocation Room 113, Friend Center Princeton, New Jersey, USA 26 October 2023

    Distributed protocols: a logical approach

    Distributed protocols are famously hard to get right, specify, and reason about. Logic can help! For example, it can help us give a three-day summer school course on a message-free, time-free, failure-free logical abstraction for specifying message-passing timed protocols with failure.

  2. Talk type: Research talk 2026
    Exponential cake and consistent controllers

    This talk treats the consistent controllers problem: suppose you have multiple interacting state machines (controllers) A, B, C, and D. Suppose controller B is bad and might equivocate, meaning that it may report different and incompatible states to peers A, C, and D. How can peers A, C, and D detect this misbehaviour and gracefully recover to a consistent state? Answers that invoke a single controlling peer G that suspends A, C, and D and resets them to a most recent consistent state are not admissible; there is no deus ex machina here, just controllers trying to stay consistent. If this problem seems hypothetical – it’s not. The world already consists of interacting controllers and the problem of consistency is a serious brake on safe progress.

    Presented by Murdoch J. Gabbay With Isaac Sheff, Anthony Hart Heliax Research Talk 17 July 2026

    Heliax Research Talk 17 July 2026

    Declarative Bracha Broadcast using 3-valued logic

    Distributed protocols are typically described using imperative pseudocode. But what if we could specify them declaratively, as logical theories? We use a three-valued logic, where the third truth-value ‘b’ represents broken/Byzantine behaviour. The result is simple and highly effective.

  4. Talk type: Workshop talk 2026
    Heterogeneous Broadcast

    A protocol is heterogeneous when different controllers may have different trust assumptions. A controller is a machine that issues state: a bank, a national register, a blockchain, etc. The world has many controllers, each of which a) have their own trust assumptions and b) must interoperate with the others. Multiple trust assumptions takes us to a distinct design space, so that Heterogeneous Bracha Broadcast is not merely a generalisation of (Homogeneous) Bracha Broadcast: it’s a different beast.

  6. Talk type: Conference talk 2025
    A shallow arithmetisation of first-order validity

    I discuss how to directly arithmetise (cryptographer-speak for ‘translate into polynomials, the language of cryptography’) validity over finite models. This means that you can specify a property – e.g. some desired correctness property – and via cryptographic magic generate succinct or zero-knowledge proofs that a model satisfies that correctness property, without communicating that model to the recipient of the proof. This is very useful, I would argue, for quickly proving correctness of data, behaviour, or anything else that can be finitely represented.

    Presented by Murdoch J. Gabbay 41st British Colloquium for Theoretical Computer Science (BCTCS 2025) Room TL325B, Learning and Teaching Building, University of Strathclyde Hosted by University of Strathclyde Glasgow, Scotland 15 April 2025

  7. Talk type: Workshop talk 2025
    Message logic for service commitments

    Message logic is a logic for specifying and reasoning about promises that participants in a message-passing distributed system can make to one another. This sounds simple but it turns out to lead to a surprisingly nice logical framework. This logic is somewhat different from the logics I’m used to studying, notably because the notion of logical implication has a measure-theoretic flavour. This comes from the fact that promises made might be broken, even in good faith, e.g. if the entire network fails.

  1. Talk type: Workshop talk 2023
    Semitopologies and semiframes for distributed heterogeneous consensus

    A semitopology is like a topology, but without the restriction that an intersection of open sets needs to be open (this arises from modelling distributed systems). Semitopologies naturally generate a three-valued logic (by considering continuous functions out of them), and they can be dualised to semiframes, which are complete join-semilattices with a compatibility relation. We study these, along with various well-behavedness conditions on points in a semitopology.

  2. Talk type: Workshop talk 2023
    Semitopology and (paraconsistent) logic

    A semitopology is like a topology, but without the restriction that an intersection of open sets needs to be open (this arises from modelling distributed systems). It turns out that semitopologies are most easily classified using a three-valued paraconsistent logic; put another way, when you try to develop a logic over semitopologies, with semantics as continuous functions, a third truth-value very naturally appears.

  3. Talk type: Seminar 2023
    Equivariance: the name of the true monster in your induction

    My PhD was all about difficulties encountered combining inductively defined syntax with variable binding. In this talk I make two arguments: first, that names are best considered a primitive datatype with specific mathematical properties; and second, that the specific property is fundamentally not the fancy stuff that most of my PhD was about, but instead it is the apparently bland assertion of equivariance, namely, the property that a name-permutation universally applied, preserves validity. Once you have equivariance, I argue, the rest of the theory drops out. Conversely, if you do not take equivariance as primitive, your treatment of names may become painful. In short: equivariance is it. For more on these ideas, see the associated paper, the Nominal Haskell package, and the Nominal Agda package.

    Presented by Murdoch J. Gabbay LAIV seminar 15 June 2023

  5. Talk type: Seminar 2023
    Semitopology: a new topological model of heterogeneous consensus

    A quorum in a distributed system is a set of participants with sufficient power to take collective action, independently from the rest of the system. Quorums are closed under arbitrary union, but not under arbitrary intersection. It turns out that if you treat this as something that is nearly (but not quite) a point-set topology, and then replay topological notions like open set, closed set, dense set, and continuous function, interpreted as quorums, then you obtain constructs with real meaning in the theory of distributed systems (e.g. a dense set corresponds to a blocking set). It turns out further that if you take notions from distributed systems and view them topologically, then further rich structure is revealed.

    Presented by Murdoch J. Gabbay Scottish Programming Languages Seminar (SPLS) Coats Building, University of the West of Scotland Paisley, Scotland 7 June 2023

  2. Talk type: Conference talk 2022
    The (semi)topology of distributed consensus

    A semitopology is like a topology, but without the restriction that an intersection of open sets needs to be open. This generalises the notion of quorum from distributed systems. It soon becomes clear that the most interesting semitopologies are those that satisfy an intersection-of-open-sets property which is the precise negation of Hausdorff separation.

  7. Talk type: Seminar 2013
    Denotation of Contextual Modal Type theory

    Nanevski in his PhD thesis introduced and studied Contextual Modal Theory Theory. This is a lambda-calculus based via the Curry-Howard correspondence on an extension of the modal logic S4 with multiple modalities, one for each variable. The application is to meta-programming, where the intuitive denotation of Box A is “syntax of type A”. The language itself is pretty, and we developed a denotational semantics with interesting properties. I will give a tour of the system and discuss future work. See also the paper on Denotations of CMTT. Thanks to César Sánchez and Aleksandar Nanevski, and thanks to Paola Huerta for the calm and efficient rescue from that first hotel.

  2. Talk type: Seminar 2012
    Three semantics for logic out of context

    It is common to reason about semantics in a context. This context may be a valuation (assigning denotations to variables) or a typing context (assigning types to variables), or a memory state (enumerating known memory), and so on. I will outline a nominal approach to semantics which subsumes context into a more abstract nominal notion of support. Using this we can give three semantics to (first-order) logic: in lattices, sets, and algebras. The full details are technical and in this talk I will try to bring out the non-technical “meaning of it all”, with an emphasis (necessarily speculative, but realistic) on practical implications to logic, specification, and programming.

    Universidad Politécnica de Madrid Madrid, Spain 11 July 2012

    Universidad Politécnica de Madrid 11 July 2012

  3. Talk type: Seminar 2012
    The algebraisation of logic using nominal techniques

    Over the past five years a number of systems, such as first-order logic and the lambda-calculus, have been algebraically axiomatised using nominal techniques. A next step is to relate these (equational) axiomatisations to order-theoretic notions such as complemented bounded lattices (a.k.a. Boolean algebras). I will talk about recent progress here, giving an order-theoretic account of first-order logic: the punchline is that it will correspond to a complemented finitely fresh-complete lattice with a substitution—wait for the talk or see my recent paper with Dowek Nominal semantics for predicate logic: algebras, substitution, quantifiers, and limits. Israel has a tradition in logical foundations. Fraenkel–the Fraenkel of Zermelo-Fraenkel and Fraenkel-Mostowski set theory–was Dean of Jerusalem University. So it was special while visiting the logic community in Israel to discover not only that they already knew the background to what I was talking about, but that also, their research had anticipated much of what I was about to say. Special thanks here to Arnon Avron.

    Tel Aviv University Tel Aviv, Israel 20 June 2012

  4. Talk type: Seminar 2012
    The application of symmetry to computing and meta-mathematics

    Symmetry has long been recognised as important in mathematics and physics, but its importance has been less appreciated in theories of logic and computation. In this (mathematically oriented, but non-technical) talk I describe what symmetry means in logic and computation, examine the benefits we can obtain by considering logic and computation as inherently “symmetric” mathematical entities, and relate this back to traditional foundations based on sets and functions. Special thanks here to Stuart Margolis and the remarkable Plotkin family.

    A talk given at CILC09, the 24th Italian Conference on Computational Logic in Ferrara, Italy. See also the associated paper. I discuss permissive-nominal terms, which are similar to nominal terms but with properties more like those of first-order syntax.   4. Talk type: Workshop talk 2008
    Two-and-a-half order lambda-calculus

    Talk given on Friday 4 July in the WFLP 2008 in Italy at 10:00. I describe two-and-a-half order lambda-calculus, a two-level lambda-calculus. Normally, the lambda-calculus has a capture-avoiding substitution. The two-level lambda-calculus is actually two lambda calculi, with distinct namespaces for variable symbols of `strong’ and `weak’ variables, but sharing a common application operator. Substitution for a strong variable does not avoid capture by lambda-abstraction for a weak variable. This leads to interesting and unusual phenomena.

    Talk given on Friday 4 April in the AISB conference in Aberdeen at 17:30. I describe a substitution action defined for the atoms on Fraenkel-Mostowski sets (the general set theory version of nominal sets). In the original Gabbay-Pitts ‘nominal’ approach to modelling syntax, the atoms in Fraenkel-Mostowski set theory were used to model variable symbols. 2005

  1. Talk type: Workshop talk 2005
    Automating first-order logic

    Given at the second CANS meeting on December 6. We present Nominal Algebraic Specifications, a theory of universal algebra based on Nominal Terms and thus able to algebraically specify, in a suitable sense, theories-with-binding. We show how an algebraic theory of first-order logic leads to “one-and-a-halfth-order logic”, which is above first-order logic and slightly to the side of second-order logic. We discuss proof-methods for the system and possible extensions. Thanks to Maribel Fernández.

  2. Talk type: Colloquium 2005
    One-and-a-halfth-order logic

    Given at the Institute for Logic, Language, and Computation, in their colloquium on mathematical logic. We present one-and-a-halfth-order logic, which is a logic somewhere above first-order logic and slightly to the side of second-order logic. It satisfies cut-elimination, has an algebraic presentation, and allows to quantify over all predicates in an interesting and unusual way. Thanks to Benedikt Loewe.

We find it to be remarkably expressive, and suggest that we can encode records, modules, objects, dynamic binding and rebinding, and many other constructs involving non-capture-avoiding substitution.

    FM and the pi-calculus

    I’ve been using FreshML to program a pet interest of mine; transition systems and bisimulation checkers for the pi-calculus (see [gabbay:thempc]). Talks by type

Software

I hope you find the following software interesting and perhaps informative. I enjoyed writing it.

Browser

Programmable slide-rule emulator

Explore a two-sided scientific slide rule with configurable scales, classic instrument layouts, and guided lessons. Move the slide and cursor, then save your own instrument for offline use.

Browser

Aperiodic Life

Cellular automata on square, hexagonal, Einstein-hat, and Penrose tilings. You can change the rules, paint a starting pattern, and watch the evolution of one of a library of curated examples. Some of those examples are new, including some novel glider shapes.

Logic

3muQL model checker

A model checker for 3muQL, for checking whether a model satisfies specified logical properties. See the related Declarative Paxos paper.

Arithmetic and logic

zkFOL

An efficient implementation of the Arithmetisation of first-order logic paper, with thanks to Andrew Mendelsohn and Jeremy Ornelas.

Haskell

Nominal Datatypes

Names, swapping, binding, and capture-avoiding programming, with examples for the lambda-calculus, System F, and EUTxO.

See also the August 2020 SPLV notes and recordings

Food intolerance

I'm wheat-intolerant: I don't get an allergic reaction to wheat, but neither can I digest it, so it just sits in my digestion until it ... comes out, eventually.

Finding things to eat is not a problem, thank goodness, but I miss out on convenience. I can't just "grab a sandwich". I have to plan ahead, just in case.

  • I can eat non-wheat carbohydrates like rice, potatoes, oats, barley, corn, and rye. Porridge, polenta, and pumpernickel are fine.
  • Nuts, milk, and soya are not a problem.
  • I can't eat pasta, pizza, cous-cous (cracked grain), naan, laffa flatbreads, doughnuts, baguettes, croissants (which is a real pity), sandwiches, or saitan (purified wheat gluten; that one is a big no-no).
  • Potato gnocchi are fine; they contain a bit of wheat but it's generally not enough to bother me. Likewise, gravy thickened with a bit of wheat flour is fine. Funnily enough, I'm generally OK with a sinfully rich chocolate cake too: that's mostly sugar, fat, and chocolate, which I can digest very well.

I usually just ask for the "gluten-free" option. It's a simplification, but a useful one in practice.
